genxml.title: SHub 2 registers outside the I/O interface, differences from SHub 1
genxml.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
genxml.doc: SHub 2 offsets as the SGI Linux ia64 platform header defines them (SH2_ names). Registers the header defines only for SHub 1 are removed; for those, SHub 2's address is not in the sources read (unknown). Field layouts not patched here are the SHub 1 ones: the header gives one set of field macros for both chips. Registers added from the SHub 2 firmware (grade and site named on each) give the 32-bit offset in the local window; add 0x2_0000_0000 for the address the firmware uses.

struct.name: X_DIMM_CFG
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: DIMM population word. One routine (0xff482c60) merges the discovered DIMM layout into the old value: the preserved bits are 38 and above and bits 7, 15, 23 and 31, so bits 37:32 are rewritten, and the same value is written to all three registers (X, Y and JNR); bits 37:36 are then set by 0xff4856b0, which reads the Y register first. Offset in the local window (add 0x2_0000_0000); the name is the PROM's own register-name table, not Linux; no source defines the reset value.

struct.name: X_CFG
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Memory controller timing word. The firmware writes the same value to X and Y: 0x4856_5320_3324_110e, built from the old Y value by clearing bit 0, setting bit 1, depositing 3 at bits 7:2, replacing bits 39:8, depositing 3, 5, 6 at bits 43:40, 47:44, 51:48, setting bits 52 and 54, clearing bit 53 (set instead when the DIMM record's word at offset 8 equals 4), depositing 0x10 at bit 55 (width 7) and setting bit 62 (sites 0xff483016 to 0xff4831a0). Only bits 39:8 have a name here; the other positions are as written. Offset in the local window (add 0x2_0000_0000); the name is the PROM's own register-name table, not Linux; no source defines the reset value.

struct.name: IPI_INT
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Send an interprocessor interrupt (processor interface or local block, inferred). The sender writes this register in the target node's global MMR window with send set, the target's physical processor id, a delivery type, a vector and a fixed base. The kernel stores through uncached physical mode with release ordering, after a memory barrier. On a SHub 1 revision 2 or lower it holds a global lock around the store and waits for the PIO write status to drain.

struct.name: RTC_INT_CONFIG
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Where the comparator interrupt of RTC 1, 2 and 3 is sent: type, target processor id, vector area and vector. The mmtimer driver writes the vector and processor id fields and leaves type, agent and base zero. The register has the same layout as the IPI message, without the send bit. A fourth comparator (RTC 0) exists; the driver comment says firmware uses it, and the header defines nothing for it.

struct.name: RTC_INT_ENABLE

struct.doc: Enable for the comparator interrupt of RTC 1, 2 and 3. The mmtimer driver disables it, sets the comparator to all ones, clears the pending bit, writes the configuration, enables, and only then writes the real expiry, in that order.

struct.name: EVENT_OCCURRED
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Pending interrupt events for the node (SHub interrupt event occurred). The kernel's interrupt acknowledge reads it, keeps the bits in the mask of the junk-bus UART, IPI and the two II interrupts, and writes that value to the alias to clear them; Linux only reads it. Bits the header names are established. SAL 5.04 reads it for the error bits (mask 0x7ef, sites 0xffa239a0 and 0xffa23fd6) and for bit 21 (site 0xffa31506), and writes bits 5 and 8 to this register itself (sites 0xffa32816 and 0xffa32996); a model should OR written bits in (inferred). Zero from reset is tolerated; the reset value is unknown. Bit 21 must read 0 for the PROM's INIT handling. See interrupts.md.

field.name: rtc0_int
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa31d96 (alias write 0x800000 right after RTC0's enable is cleared)

field.name: bit21
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa31506 (read), 0xffa31566 (clear through the alias, 0x200000)

field.name: bit8
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa32816 (write to the register), 0xffa23a20 (mask 0x7ef)

field.name: bit5
field.from: SAL 5.04 PROM site 0xffa32996 (write to the register), 0xffa23a20 (mask 0x7ef)

struct.name: EVENT_OCCURRED_ALIAS
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Clears pending events: the kernel writes the bits it wants cleared here and never reads it. That a one clears and a zero leaves a bit alone is inferred from the kernel writing back exactly the bits it read as set (interrupt acknowledge) and a single bit to clear one RTC event (the mmtimer driver). Neither the kernel nor the header says what a read returns.

struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Junk bus LED registers, one per processor slice (header SH1_REAL_JUNK_BUS_LED0 to 3, 64 KiB apart). The kernel keeps an 8-bit LED state per processor and stores it with a 16-bit write at LED0 plus slice times 64 KiB: bit 0 is the heartbeat, toggled twice a second from the timer interrupt, bit 1 an activity flag. The junk bus also holds the UART whose interrupt is event_occurred bit 20.

struct.name: PTC
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Purge translation cache message, SHub 2 (header SH2_PTC). One 64-bit store per target node replaces SHub 1's two. The region id and region number do not go in the data: the kernel adds them, shifted left by four, to the register's address. (The header's `SH2_PTC_ADDR_SHFT` is 4 but sits under a region-id comment and no kernel code uses it, which uses `SH2_PTC_RID_SHFT`; the data's address field is `SH2_PTC_ADDR_MASK`, which starts at bit 12, and that is what this file uses.) The data carries the type bit, the page size and the start bit, and the virtual address in bits 60:12. How wide the address-encoded part is, and so how large the register window is, is unknown. The kernel only waits on the PIO write status afterwards; on a deadlock it reads the status alias instead of clearing it.

struct.name: RTC
struct.from: Linux v5.3 SGI SN2 platform MMR header (GPL): names, offsets and field positions; kernel use from the same tree's SN2 setup, interrupt, I/O, timer, SMP and TLB-purge code and the v4.9 real-time clock driver
struct.doc: Real-time clock: a 55-bit counter, read by the kernel as its clock source (clock source rating 450, mask 55 bits) and for microsecond delays, because the CPU cycle counters are not synchronised across processors. The frequency is not in a register; the kernel asks firmware for it. The driver comment says the clock registers sit alone on a 64 KiB page, which is what lets user space map it read-only. The SHub 1 PROM (SAL 5.04) writes 0 to it at the SAL_B reset entry (0xffa94d20) and again to a node's counter in the interconnect phase, then reads it on every delay and timeout, so it must advance. Its tick period comes from rtc_ctl (SHub 1: 10 ns times the field plus one, 50 ns after the PROM's own write). See prom-reset.md.
